title: To obey is better (1 Samuel 15:22)
hook: "to obey is better than sacrifice"; Saul chose the showy offering
tomorrow: The Lord looketh on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saul, the tall new king crouched behind the luggage at Mizpah. Your line was he hid among the baggage. Today, Saul is king, and he's not hiding anymore.

"Blessed be thou of the LORD; I have performed the commandment of the LORD." That's how Saul greets Samuel, back from war against Amalek. Job done, as far as he's concerned. On the way home he has even set up a monument for himself at Carmel. Samuel asks one quiet question. What then is this bleating of sheep in my ears, and the lowing of oxen that I hear? Saul had been told to leave nothing of Amalek's, and here are the best of the sheep and cattle, alive, bleating in the background of his victory speech.
screen: `I HAVE PERFORMED THE COMMANDMENT.` → `A MONUMENT AT CARMEL.` → `WHAT IS THIS BLEATING OF SHEEP?`

segments.voice: Saul has an answer ready. The people spared the best of the sheep and oxen, he says, to sacrifice to the LORD your God; the rest we destroyed. The command against Amalek is hard to read, a command to destroy everything, and this lesson won't pretend otherwise. But the chapter's own question is narrower: Saul was told one thing, did another, then dressed it up as worship. Samuel answers. Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt-offerings and sacrifices, as in hearkening to his voice? "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams." To obey, and to hearken. In Hebrew, the word for obey here is the verb for hear, the same verb as in Shema, hear, O Israel. A few days ago, a boy in the sanctuary said speak, for thy servant heareth. Now a king is told that hearing is worth more than the fattest offering. Then Saul admits it: I have sinned, because I feared the people, and hearkened to their voice. He did hearken, just to the wrong voice. And as Samuel turns to go, Saul asks: honor me now, I pray, before the elders of my people. Even his apology wants an audience. The prophet Hosea sounds a similar note later: God desires mercy, and not sacrifice. But here it's one king, a monument, and some bleating sheep he hoped no one would hear.
screen: `THE BEST WAS SAVED FOR SACRIFICE.` · `OBEY MEANS HEAR.` · `I FEARED THE PEOPLE.` · `HONOR ME BEFORE THE ELDERS.` · then, large: `TO OBEY IS BETTER THAN SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Think of one plain thing someone has actually asked of you lately, a partner, a parent, a friend, your own body: the dishes, the phone call, the apology without a speech. Notice whether part of you would rather make a grander gesture, and choose the plain thing. If you pray, hold Samuel's words: to obey is better than sacrifice.
Shema. The Hebrew verb for hear and obey, the same word Samuel used when he told Saul that obeying is worth more than the fattest offering.
Your line: do the plain thing. No monument needed, and no audience. Day seven hundred thirty-three, done.

screen: `DAY 733 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LORD LOOKETH ON THE HEART.`

howItsDone: Jews read Saul's war with Amalek as part of the Former Prophets, and Samuel's line that to obey is better than sacrifice is studied as a teaching about what God asks.

chat.says: Saul saved the best animals to sacrifice to God. Why was Samuel so upset about it?
options: He did what he wasn't told, then called it worship. Hearing God matters more than any sacrifice.
Samuel wanted the best animals for his own household, and was angry Saul kept them.
Saul brought the wrong kind of animals, since only sheep could be offered to God.
chat.meaning: Samuel says to obey is better than sacrifice. In Hebrew, obey is the verb hear, as in Shema; Saul heard the people instead.

Amalek.meaning: the enemy Saul was sent to fight

Carmel.meaning: where Saul set up a monument to himself

Shema.meaning: hear; the same Hebrew verb also means obey

Hosea.meaning: a later prophet: God desires mercy, and not sacrifice
